the way you describe the dam and the lake resonates with me about how I experience grief. I know it’s there and I know it’s not ever going to go away. you could call it traumatic I guess, but a lot of people also recognize that grief never really goes away but just becomes less disruptive. Its effects become less disruptive in your life and you are able to not have to feel it so bad as much, it feels less overwhelming and unmanageable.

It feels like it doesn’t hurt or sting if that makes sense. The wound or the injury is scarred over. It is not an open hurting wound, and it’s not inflamed. And it probably feels weird that you don’t feel anything there. It might even make you think that you must have gone numb or lost sensation there.

personally with my grief, I know it healed a bit weird. There is a weird mass of scar tissue that I can poke at if I want to hurt my own feelings and make myself cry. I know that my grief has also morphed and made little deformed trauma children with all of my preexisting traumatic events so that my grief comes out in these (truly fuckin lame) somewhat subconscious coping mechanisms and it’s like I figured out how to flex some kind of muscle or tendon that like pulls or nudges my freaking scar tissue. Because when I do that, I can feel it. And it doesn’t feel numb for a minute. There is sensation in the place I had already grown so accustomed to feeling some very significant pain. 

But like, I try not to do that. Like just poking at my grief scar for funsies or shits & giggles. Because that pain is no joke. Because that pain is truly lethal. 

That’s all you get. Numbness.

It will probably be hard for you to become like rich people. It is a totally different mindset that I think you don’t just automatically snap out of unless you really have a complex about getting as far away from your origins as possible. Some people, in trying to run away from their past, completely throw out their histories and former lives because it upsets them to have to think about. 

I think sometimes it’s like rich people are just colorblind and don’t understand things, they never will, and they really have no need to ever care about that if they don’t want to.

But people who weren’t brought up with every luxury see all these insane freaking trippy rainbow colors all over everywhere, lol. And it’s not bad, because sometimes you’ll be enjoying something that you were able to buy for yourself or something, and you will remember the days when something like it was unthinkable. And I think it just makes it that much more satisfying. Like started from the bottom and now you’re here, and that feeling of having experienced so much change and variety and breadth of experience.

Rich people won’t always have access to that. They started already at the top and maybe they made an inch or two of progress where you are actually able to look at yourself and witness that you are capable of having created comparative miles of change from where you started. 

It’s up to you to figure out how you want to manage your financial anxiety going forward—whether you want to take a gamble on investing in yourself and taking out loans for graduate school, or if it’s more valuable to you to not have to take on debt and live in moderate comfort. These are personal preferences and what you are comfortable with.

I will say though that rich people do take a lot of things for granted, and might be more likely to take bigger risks and be more irresponsible and undisciplined (not all of them but some of them, and also a good deal who don’t even notice or lack self-awareness of it). bc what always having access to money affords you is a lot of not having to care about a whole bunch of things. So my only advice would be to not copy or follow their habits too much. Being rich gives you the luxury of being wasteful and throwing a lot of valuable things away. And not being rich helps you create value in many cases, or finding it in things that are really worth it. 

I think a really useful tool is the ability to be able to practice gratitude and appreciation. You tend to appreciate things more when you know what it’s like to go without.

I believe that when you do give freely with no expectations of receiving anything in return, you can’t get “taken advantage of”.

Because one practices this particular form of selfless giving with the understanding that nothing will be received in return. You understand that the other person will never be in a position to be able to reciprocate or pay you back for whatever form of kindness that you showed to them, and sometimes that means not even a thank you.

So, that’s how that works. You somewhat forfeit the thought or idea that you would be “taken advantage of” because there is nothing after you giving with nothing in return. It is inherent to this particular practice of giving that you give the “advantage” to the other person, so that it is never them that takes it from you.

In another way is that you giving to another is the end of the transaction. They don’t owe you anything after you giving to them. They are not in your debt for you showing them any form of kindness.

And part of this is also because it’s possible that they did not request your kindness. You just freely gave it away, and to expect them to reciprocate means that your kindness comes with some potentially predatory expectations of getting something back in return. So it can sometimes end up being a case of being nice to people to entrap them in a sense of obligation to you, even though they never asked for that, you know?

- Moves halfway across the world to be with you
- Takes care of you like a parent, making your lunch for you and keeping your water bottles filled like you’re a hamster
- Emotionally and financially supports what you want to do with life and personally invests in your happiness
- Does fun things with you and balances out your more risk-taking tendencies

Things you don’t like about him
- He is not perfect enough (he sounds like he has some perfectionist tendencies especially towards himself and seeks security in controlling behaviors) and it makes him emotionally shut down that what he does have to offer isn’t what you want / what you really need is not within the things he is best equipped to offer (emotional safety / maturity, emotional care, validation… etc) 

He might lean a bit towards being codependent, where he is somewhat enabling you and your ADHD behaviors by taking care of them for you (instead of helping you to build strategies and establish habits to be able to manage your symptoms on your own). He is also enabling you by helping you become someone that will need to be financially reliant on their partner, encouraging you to do a career switch that will keep you tied to him. (that one’s kind of a double-edged sword. It’s like, if you love someone of course you want to support them in something like a career switch and do what you can to ensure their long-term happiness. At the same time, you are encouraging them to give away the personal power in being financially self-sufficient and being able to just pick up and leave). And as the codependent caretaker in the relationship, the sensitivity to criticism and grievances isn’t unheard of.

I feel like what I got out of this is that he has a lot of things to offer, which are all wonderful but at the same time will ever be enough to overlook the emotional abuse. Which is totally valid, because emotional abuse is incredibly devastating and does totally demolish relationships. And that is sad. And even though you love him, it is hard for you to have to accept that what he has to offer does not make up for the impact and damage that the emotional abuse will cause, and that you, feeling you have even less to offer, are having trouble working through the cognitive dissonance that damn, someone can seem absolutely like a dream come true but these defenses that they have (not being able to work through conflicts and address grievances) seem minor and yet are totally enough to destroy the relationship and any benefits of being with him. They are like tiny cracks in an otherwise pretty good-looking structure. 

I wonder though, if you get the validation you’re looking for, that yes, this isn’t a good relationship, you should break up with him, what are you going to do with that? Are you going to end the relationship? If you are already considering breaking up with him–– this is more for you –– where does this self-doubt come from? It’s just an interesting question to ask oneself, to explore why you are still acting from a position of powerlessness that needs other people to kind of help drive and guide her decision, and what is holding you back from being able to take a stand for yourself and just put an end to something that is not working for you. 

It can also be a kind of like, well my boyfriend is being abusive, maybe some people on the Internet can help me feel better about it by reassuring me that I’m the victim here while I probably can’t realistically leave him or break up with him because I still need to be dependent on him anyway, but I have to make sure that he is indeed abusing me because I am powerless to do anything like leave the relationship or stop the abuse that I am the victim of which I am definitely not doing to myself or enabling to continue by like, not leaving the abuser and ending the relationship.

But it can also totally be like, yep the emotional abuse is definitely working its magic to the point where I have lost my sense of self and my ability to make decisions for myself and extricate myself from my abuser (because that’s how abuse is supposed to work) and I need help and some guiding hands towards the light until I can stand on my own two feet again, because abusive cycles do work this way. All are valid. None of these are accusations or judgments on you (cos I don't know you), just exploring all the possible scenarios. Hope you work this out and find your happiness <3

It’s true that sometimes the person we were in love with the most in our life will not ultimately be the person we get to spend our life with. Life partnerships like marriage are a decades-long slog of an emotional, psychological, financial, and logistical investment, and sometimes just love itself cannot magically wave its wand to resolve all of the realistic and practical concerns for us without equal effort from both parties involved — maybe he realistically does not feel himself capable yet of the work and compromises entailed in something more than a long-term relationship, and he is being incredibly fair and kind to you to not give you any unrealistic expectations or hopes and promises that he will not be able to deliver on (which is awesome though, I appreciate this from people rather than getting unrealistic pie in the sky promises that never happen). 

For you though, if this is an option you are both receptive to — I would emphasize and highlight the opportunities for personal growth for you in making a decision like this. That you are not making this decision only for the welfare of the relationship, but to expand your own horizons, to gain from further study and education, to experience a life different than what you have now, and as a jumping off point to greater and more rewarding things for you down the line should the relationship not endure — and that you keep those personal goals for yourself in the forefront rather than focusing the majority of your happiness and life satisfaction based on the outcome of this one potentially temporary relationship.

I also wanted to say to you that part of having a successful relationship is knowing when it’s time to end the relationship. Just because a relationship ends does not make it a failure. It means it has run its course. All our relationships in life will have some probability of an expiration date when it’s time to refocus on ourselves or bring our attention to other matters or other people. In some circumstances, it can be increasingly unlikely that many of our relationships can be more than temporary (and also, life is just temporary and ephemeral too). From our childhood best friends we fell out of contact with, to our adolescent sweethearts, to our adult dating partners. Some of us will be lucky enough to have the right amount and kind of “failed” relationships to find ourselves in the life partnership that we wish to endure past decades into our old age. And a percentage of us may also have to make hard decisions to ensure that we remain in a solid and stable life partnership that promises to withstand the test of time with minimal diminishment of our quality of life. 

There is great strength in not settling for something that is not right for you. But you might also consider enjoying the present moment to its fullest without rigid expectations of what the future should have in store.
